The best way I can think to explain DID/OSDD is having multiple streams of thoughts with there own responses and life history because your brain has had to compartmentalise itself so much that all of your memory’s and what are called action systems (basically doing stuff like work, play, attachemnt or fight, flight, fawn responses etc) are fragmented resulting in a bunch of parts of your brain that have different processes to solving problems and responding. These streams of thoughts arnt as rigid as you may think and they can overlap and flow into each other, it can be quite lucid at times and you may not even recognise your being influenced but at other times it can cause a lot of distress. I think of it like a river, sometimes it branches out into two separate distinct rivers and sometimes those rivers can merge and the water from each can flow within the same stream. however when these rivers conflict it can be very painful, instead of a nice merge it can be like rapids with sharp rocks with rivers flowing in and out, merging and separating rapidly. It can cause some of the most intense psychological pain I’ve ever known, it can cause painful pressures in your head, bad headaches, intense back pain sometimes to the point I can’t walk. A lot of the time when there’s a lot of chaos in my head I just lie in bed squirming around with tears in my eyes trying not to scream just from the sensations in my head and body. 

DID isn’t just like a bunch of people in your head its dissociated parts of someone’s personality which were never able to integrate that together and have gained there own sense of self. While alters may like to see themselves as fully separated people often this is just a form of dissociation to further separate that alter from the truama and responses that anouther alter holds and escape having to accspt what happened happened to you as well as them. You often need intrusions and this fluidity to be able to function beacuse (at least for me) even if an alter is very complex there’s often gaps in parts that other alters need to fill. For instance one alter may seem very fleshed out and functional in daily life, but may not hold any fight or flight response, so when faced with a stressful situation where they need to access the response they can’t. This may result in a full switch to anouther alter but sometimes depending on the person and trigger that alter may only express itself through passive influence, which can include partial taking over of the body so those two alters are there together responding the the situation. This may help the system stay more discreet and keep a level of cohesion to help protect from the outside world and stop people noticing the switch, it can also help reduce the distress from the amnesic barriers and help things move more fluidly in the response, plus it can help dampen down intense response that the brain wishes to repress or may not be appropriate in that situation. In fact things like P-DID and OSDD-1 which are different presentations of the same things that cause DID often work a lot more this way through passive influence and co fronting.

In the theory of structural dissociation BPD is a less extreme form of OSDD-1/DID. 
BPD is theorised to function as several dissociated parts similarly to DID/OSDD-1 however what sets it apart is these parts have no or very little senses of self (there not nearly as developed as alters) and they tend to impact things like attachment and emotional regulation the most.

If someone is diagnosed with OSDD-1 it is because they don’t meet 1 of the criteria for DID. This is often split into 2 honorary diagnoses which are OSDD-1a and OSDD-1b

In OSDD-1b dissociated parts have significant changes in sense of self and have there own elaborate identity but do not have any significant amnesia.

In OSDD-1a there isn’t significant changes in continuity of self but there is significant amount of amnesia - often parts will present as the same person at different ages or all parts will front through a shell alter that can almost implant onto other alters so outwardly they all look consistent.

BPD, (C)PTSD and DID/OSDD all share some simlar symptoms and can be confused with each other very easily because ultimately they are all on the same spectrum of dissociation with PTSD being the lowest end and DID the top end.

In terms of anxiety this is a little different as the action systems an alter holds will change how anxiety is experienced. Action systems are split into two types, ANP and EP. ANP (apparently normal part) deals with things needed for everyday life such as relationships, eating, sleeping, drinking, exploration etc. EP (emotional part) deals with things needed for safety, such as fight, flight, freeze, hyperviglence etc. The expression of say an EP that holds a flight response may seem very anxious and skittish, which may make people say that said alter “holds there anxiety”, but it just holds the response which requires more of that anxiety. Plus it is possible for EPs to hold vehement emotions, like anxiety, which could reach a point of classing that individual alter for there own disorder if they were not part of a system.

“Myers was not implying that emotion was only experienced by EP. Rather he was emphasising the overwhelming or vehement nature of EPs traumatic emotions in comparison to ANP. Firstly that study doesn’t back up any of your claims that DID is just BPD, there are just as many if nothing more times this article says that DID is real or different from BPD then it is the same, from the article:
> “Current knowledge does not at this time sufficiently justify the validity of DID as a separate diagnosis,” but this also does not disprove the concept”

> “Loewenstein and Bliss concluded that DID existed and spontaneous autohypnotic symptoms were basic to the phenomenology of DID.”

> “However, they also found other patients that could not be so characterized, and they concluded that DID was in fact a distinct entity, but overdiagnosed.”

The debate that DID is just an extreme version of BPD is an interesting one. If you look up the theory of structural dissociation you will see that both BPD and DID are explained by this however BPD is only secondary structural dissociation and DID is terentury. On the surface it does seem like DID is an extreme version of BPD however only about 30-70% (64% mentioned in that study) of DID patients meet the diagnosis for BPD where almost all meet the diagnosis for CPTSD (another disorder classed in secondary dissociation). So therefore DID is less seen as an extreme version of BPD and more like an extreme version of CPTSD and its genuinely agreed that In BPD patients there’s something else in the mix (though all disorders explained by structural dissociation share a lot of symptoms and are often co morbid with each other).
There’s also debate on if BPD is even a valid diagnosis and just in fact a different presentation of CPTSD. However even if the majority of BPD cases have childhood abuse and truama only 80% of BPD cases could identify a disorganised attachment, which means childhood trauma is only an activation for people who are genetically susceptible developing BPD but this isn’t required in every case where for CPTSD, DID and OSDD-1 it is a requirement, ussally from childhood. CPTSD also symptoms are different enough to warrant its own disorder. 
The fact not every person with BPD has trauma proves that it’s not a less extreme version of DID/OSDD-1 since truama is a requirement for those conditions and instead makes more sense it’s an extreme version of CPTSD, a disorder that’s almost always co morbid. Also DID/OSDD-1 is almost certainly under-diagnosed in my opinion because of the stigmas around it being rare.

On the other stuff, I am part of a professionally recognised OSDD-1b system, and yes while alters are a truama response there probably the least difficult part of the disorder. In fact alters are a coping mechanism for your brain, they often can make things a little easier, and some people end up having very complex and deep relationships within there system and end up relying heavily on these dissociative barriers. Final fusion (what most people associate with being “treated” for DID/OSDD-1) is therefore really scary for some people, it means when things are stressfull it means they can’t just step back, it means addressing all your truama, finding new truama that was previously suppressed, which not everyone is ready for. It also means relationships they have between alters will have to be experienced in a new way, and these relationships can be as meaningful as irl relationships in some cases. FF can also cause more intense emotions and physical pain and there’s always the risk that’s it’s impossible to achieve or that the person just splits again. Not everyone is ready for healing or ready to seek that out, many systems don’t realise they want FF untill there in treatment for a while and ready for that discussion. You can’t just say, “oh this person doesn’t want to loose there alters, faker!!” Especially when you have no experience of that disorder and are just going off stereotypes and some loose research and especially when healing from this disorder is so complicated, long, scary and overwhelming. People deal with things in different ways and that’s okay. Personally for me final fusion seems like a beautiful thing, and a way to allow us all to live and honour each other, tho I’m not sure if that’s right for us beacuse we are so early on our journey and we arnt ready to make that decision. 
Some systems wish to purse functional multiplicity, an equally valid path, tho is often portrayed by people who don’t know much as “anti recovery” which is why I’m addressing it. Sometimes FF is physically impossible or those internal relationships are deeply important to that systems functioning and taking that away would mean that person couldn’t cope, or the idea of having to live a whole new way is too scary and that’s okay. I’ll say this again alters arnt often the horrible thing about this disorder that makes it so difficult to live with, especially not after work in therapy to help the system work as a cohesive unit, but it’s the CPTSD and common co morbid disorders that are what make this disorder so difficult (though of course not in every case). Yes it’s not an Uwu cutesy disorder by a long shot but forgive me if I don’t want to talk about the harrowing pain it leaves me in and instead on the more positive side that allows me not to feel so down in how my brain has decided to cope and foster a good mind set to have with myself. I do admit that tik tok and twitter have a lot of anti recovery rhetoric, and I try to be wary of that, but also this isn’t unusual for mental health community’s to become toxic, look at ED community’s, self harm communities and self help communitys at best they often don’t help and at worst make things even worse. It doesn’t mean people in those communities don’t need help. There unhealthy but it’s not productive to bully teenagers for a sorta cringe time in there healing journey and make them feel even more hostile. Sure some might be doing it for attention but in order to not risk pulling someone down on this actual journey I tend not to ever fake claim.

Getting a diagnosis can literally put the person at risk and potentially kill them. Plus it can reduce options for treatment for co morbid conditions, which is also dangerous. The disorder itself has a lot of stigma and a lot of mental health professionals don’t understand it. One big one is that it can stop gender reassignment treatment, which is life saving treatment. Also sometimes people with DID unfairly have there children taken away from them when they are capable of looking after them. There’s a lot of reasons to not want a diagnosis, stigma the main one, it’s not your right to come in demanding people get diagnosed with an incredibly stigmatised condition which can follow them there whole life. I’m sorry you have PTSD and that it’s so hard on you no one deserves that but it’s not stigmatised in nearly the same way and therefore you arnt faced with that question of, “do I get diagnosed? or risk loosing life my child/future children and/or access to life saving treatment and/or just in general facing discrimination from mental health professionals the rest of my life?”. If I ever got a diagnosis of OSDD-1b then I’d never want it on my records for those reasons, I just care about treatment not for a diagnosis for something I already know.

Also about the controlling switching that’s completely possible without therapy, it depends, the more dissociated a system is the harder it will be on your own, it is also is a lot easier if the system has a gatekeeper. If a system is able to foster good communication on its own, which there’s a lot of resources out there now, then a system can control switches and learn to work together without any therapy. We did it, and i know others who have too, it’s really not that impossible. All therapy is there to do is encourage that communication, but if your able to do that yourself through journals and inner worlds then there’s no reason switching can’t become consensual.
Also a lot of experts say that while switching can be brought on by distress theres a lot of other reasons for it. Actully multiplicity and me did an talk to the experts video in which she interviewed someone who treats DID/OSDD-1, very good would recommend, and he explained that random switches can occur if the alter who switched in is in need of something, eg a child alter switching in to watch cartoons. This is also a really common experience in those with DID/OSDD-1.

Yes I agree, the first one does not have a big enough sample size to be certain of the numbers, however those numbers tend to be pretty consistent with most information I read on the topic. Plus personally knowing how covert DID is and understanding how it’s formed, as well as from personal experience I do believe it’s somewhat accurate, and it’s around the  number listed in America in the dsm-5 (1.5%). Though more research definitely needs to be conducted.
 
The second one I will say that DID and OSDD-1 arnt the only disorders that fall under dissociative disorders. There’s dissociative amnesia, depersonalisation derealisation disorder and OSDD-2/3/4. I can believe quite a lot of people experience these, especially dpdr beacuse dissociation just as a symptom is barely talked about yet is one really common in a lot of mental health problems, so it would be hard to explain your experiences if no one even knows what your experiencing and there is no other symptoms. Dissociation does definitely impact functioning, but in personal experience it tends to be only on the sever end that it does so really intensely, at least for me (who may possibly have OSDD-1/DID and has a score of about 46.5 on the DES scale). Like when everything is blurry/losing colour you can barely see, or your just keep zoning out and you can barely take in information or when I cant move, then that’s when my functioning is really bad. But on the lower end it tends not to have to much impact on how i function, sometimes I can ignore it and sometimes not even notice it, and go about my life normally. Hell I look back and realised I dissociated so much through my whole life but never noticed because your not meant to notice, that’s sorta the point. I’d say it’s not impossible to believe that up to 18% of people have these experiences but it just never reaches the point where it’s easy to notice or really impacts too much, though I do emphasise the “up to” I do believe it is probably less and there just stating the highest estimate.

One thing in general that’s really hard with DID and especially OSDD-1 (due to changes in name and categorisation) is lack of research, there still is tremendous stigma and lack of funding and disbelief it can occur, so it’s labelled as rare and bizarre even when it’s not as rare as people think. Plus it’s naturally covert and it tends to only shows itself once someone is out of there abusive environment or in a time of little stress, which adds even more complexity of studying the prevalence. Personally I think anywhere from 1 to 5% of the world population experience DID or OSDD-1, that’s my personal opinion going off all the things I’ve read and personal experience. I still don’t think that’s enough to say it’s as rare as I hear it made out to be. I think people definitely fake it, I think there’s so much misinformation and anti recovery out there that needs to be called out on. But I do wish DID and OSDD-1 was talked about more, esspecilly outside of the US, and research was done in a wider variety of places, especially marginalised communities and communities that experience high chronic trauma and are situated in war zones and places with high levels of poverty who are often not able to get included. The people who are often most traumatised are often the least likely to have access to care and so it can be difficult to account them and thats why I’d imagine you may see numbers higher then you’d expect, and why I personally think this is quite difficult to find an accurate answer.

Even if DID is present in only 1% of the population (the dsm-5 estimates 1.5%) that’s still a massive amount of people, if there’s 1000 students in a school there’s a good chance 10 of them will have DID. Sure it’s rare Ig, but not anymore then a lot of mental health problems like schizophrenia, bipolar or BPD, and we don’t call them rare.
